lesson.title: Filling In the Unknown Region: Solving Backward With Venn Diagrams
lesson.summary: When a problem gives you the individual probabilities and the chance of neither event, you can combine the complement idea with the general addition rule to solve for the overlap, then fill in every other region by subtraction.
lesson.body:
Problems do not always hand you the overlap probability directly the way the Spanish and French example did. More often you are given P(A), P(B), and P(neither), and you have to work backward to find P(A and B) before you can finish the diagram. The strategy has two moves. First, use the complement: P(A or B) equals 1 minus P(neither), since "at least one of A or B" and "neither" split the entire sample space between them. Second, plug that result into the general addition rule and solve algebraically for the one unknown, the overlap.

Here is a worked example. At a school, P(a student plays a sport) is 0.55, P(a student is in band) is 0.30, and P(a student does neither) is 0.20. Find the probability a student does both.

Start with the complement: P(sport or band) equals 1 minus 0.20, which is 0.80. Now use the general addition rule: 0.80 equals 0.55 plus 0.30 minus P(both), which simplifies to 0.80 equals 0.85 minus P(both). Solving, P(both) equals 0.85 minus 0.80, which is 0.05.

Once you know the overlap, the rest of the Venn diagram falls out by simple subtraction, working from the inside of the diagram outward. Sport only is 0.55 minus 0.05, which is 0.50. Band only is 0.30 minus 0.05, which is 0.25. The overlap itself is 0.05, and neither was already given as 0.20. Check that all four regions cover the whole sample space: 0.50 plus 0.25 plus 0.05 plus 0.20 equals 1.00, exactly as it should.

The general habit worth keeping is to fill in the intersection first, since every other region is defined in terms of it, then let the rest of the diagram follow almost automatically. This is the same "solve for the piece you're missing, then work outward" instinct you used when reversing a tree diagram, just applied to circles instead of branches.
